Top findings all 2, most significant first

#1

Timeout-driven retransmissions — 10.11.11.5 → 10.12.12.2

R05 Significant confirmed

22 segments retransmitted after timeout, costing 5.5s of transfer time. Retransmission rate on this path is 34.4% against a capture-wide median of 0%.

Frames 157, 160, 163, 166, 169, 172, 175, 178 (8 shown of 22 occurrences)

Check next: sustained loss on the path between these hosts. This is more disruptive than the fast-retransmit pattern in R06 — the sender stalled waiting for a timer rather than recovering from duplicate ACKs.

#2

Loss in one direction only — 10.11.11.5 → 10.12.12.2

R08 Worth noting confirmed

34.4% of segments retransmitted client-to-server, against 1.1% server-to-client on the same connection. Loss is not symmetric.

Frames 157, 160, 163, 166, 169, 172, 175, 178 (8 shown of 22 occurrences)

Check next: something specific to the forward path — asymmetric routing, a congested uplink, or a policer applied in one direction. Symmetric loss would point at the shared path instead.

Checks not performed, and why

Rendered rather than dropped. A report that looks clean because half the checks never ran will close a ticket on a fault that is still live. This is the same coverage the application itself shows; the export carries it because a reader here has no other way to know what was left unexamined.

R04 · not assessed Not assessed: server response time for 5 server endpoints with fewer than 5 completed request/response exchanges. Percentiles over that few samples would not describe a distribution.
R15 · not assessed Not assessed: whether the capture host dropped packets before writing them. The classic pcap format has no field to record it, so this file cannot say either way. Packets dropped by the capturing machine look the same as packets lost on the network. If that distinction matters here, re-capturing in pcapng format would record the count.

Checks that ran

RuleNameWhat it looks for
R01zero-window-stallA receiver advertised a zero window having previously advertised non-zero, blocking the sender until a window update arrived.
R02syn-unansweredA connection attempt received no answer at all — no acceptance and no refusal — despite the client retrying.
R03syn-rejectedA connection attempt was answered with a refusal rather than an acceptance — the host is reachable, and nothing is listening on that port.
R04server-response-outlierA server:port took materially longer to begin responding than its peers in the same capture, with network round-trip time subtracted.
R05rto-retransmissionSegments were retransmitted after a timer-shaped quiet gap with no duplicate ACKs asking for them — the sender stalled waiting for a timeout.
R06fast-retransmissionSegments were retransmitted after three or more duplicate ACKs — packet loss the connection recovered from quickly.
R07out-of-order-not-lossSegments arrived out of sequence within milliseconds and in original transmission order by IP ID — reordering on the path, not packet loss.
R08asymmetric-lossRetransmission rate on one flow was at least five times higher in one direction than the other, with at least 20 retransmissions — loss is not symmetric.
R09reset-mid-transferA connection was terminated by reset while data was still moving, rather than closed cleanly once both sides were done.
R14connection-churnThe same client opened and closed many short-lived connections to one server:port instead of reusing them, paying the handshake cost each time.
R15capture-qualityReports what the capture itself may limit: flows already open when the capture began, connections seen in one direction only, and packets the capture host dropped before writing them.

4 of the fifteen v1 rules are not implemented in this build and were therefore not looked for at all. They are not listed above because listing them as "skipped" would imply a decision was made per capture; none was.
